title: ML Workflow & Data Preprocessing
oneLiner: Getting data into shape before any model sees it: types, quality, cleaning, sampling, scaling and features.

what.html:
Data preprocessing is everything you do to raw data so a model can learn from it. That means fixing mistakes, filling gaps, removing duplicates, putting numbers on comparable scales, and choosing or building the right features.

Everyday versionCooking. The recipe (the algorithm) matters, but if the vegetables are unwashed, half-missing and cut into wildly different sizes, the dish fails anyway. Preprocessing is washing, chopping and measuring.

The worked examples split it into data engineering (raw → prepared data) and feature engineering (prepared data → the features the model expects).

why.html:
• Garbage in, garbage out. A salary of −10, an age that disagrees with a birthday, or 1 January as everyone's birthday will mislead any model.
  • Every ML algorithm has three parts: data representation, parameter optimisation, and evaluation. Representation comes first and often matters most.
  • Many algorithms are sensitive to scale. Without scaling, "income in rupees" drowns out "age in years".
  • In practice it is a loop: understand the domain → integrate and clean data → learn → interpret → deploy, then back round again.

how.title: Data = objects described by attributes
how.html: Each row is an object (a record, sample, instance): a customer, a transaction. Each column is an attribute (a feature, variable): refund, marital status, income.

how.title: Know your attribute type
how.html:
• Nominal: just names, no order (zip code, colour).
  • Ordinal: ordered labels (small/medium/large, grades).
  • Interval: differences mean something, zero doesn't (°C, calendar dates).
  • Ratio: true zero, so "twice as much" makes sense (length, counts, Kelvin).

Attributes are also discrete (countable: zip codes, counts; binary is a special case) or continuous (real numbers: height, temperature).

how.title: Data comes in many shapes
how.html: Tables of records, shopping baskets (transactions), word counts per document, social networks, location data, time series and sequences such as DNA. Each needs a different representation. Watch for dimensionality (many columns), sparsity (mostly zeros), resolution (patterns depend on scale) and size.

how.title: What can be wrong with data
how.html:
Good data is correct, complete, consistent, trustworthy, interpretable and available on demand. Common problems: noise (a crackly phone line distorting a voice), outliers (values far from the rest), wrong or fake data, missing values, and duplicates.

Is it a mistake or a millionaire?An income of 10,000K might be a typo, or a genuinely rich customer. For fraud or intrusion detection, the unusual cases are exactly what you're looking for.

how.title: Aggregate: summarise many rows into fewer
how.html: Daily sales from every store can be grouped into weekly totals per city. The pattern is split–apply–combine: split rows by a key, apply a summary (mean, sum), combine the results.

how.title: Clean: fix errors, fill gaps, remove duplicates
how.html:
Remove or correct corrupt values, reconcile inconsistent codes (ratings that changed from 1–3 to A–C), drop records missing too many fields, and remove duplicate entries.

For missing values you can fill with 0, the last known value, the average, or a smooth interpolation. The demo shows how different each choice looks on a monthly series.

how.title: Spot outliers with a fence
how.html:
• IQR fence: take the middle 50% of the data (from the 25th to the 75th percentile). Anything more than 1.5 × that width beyond either end is suspicious.
  • 3-sigma rule: for bell-shaped data, almost everything (99.7%) lies within 3 standard deviations of the mean.

The main demo below lets you try both fences.

how.title: Pick a fair sample and split it
how.html:
Train, validate and test on separate parts. A sample is only useful if it is representative: it has roughly the same mix as the full data. Too few points gives noisy results; a flawed process gives bias however big the sample.

  • Random sampling: everyone has an equal chance.
  • Stratified: keep each group's share the same (e.g. each flower species).
  • Clustered: sample whole groups.
  • Imbalanced data (rare fraud): under-sample the majority or over-sample the rare class.

how.title: Put features on the same scale
how.html:
Normalisation squeezes values into a fixed range such as 0–1. It suits data with known bounds and algorithms that make no distribution assumptions (k-NN, neural nets).

Standardisation turns values into "how many standard deviations from the average". It is unbounded and less affected by outliers.

Golden rule: learn the scaling from the training data only, then apply that same scaling to the test data.

how.title: Engineer better features
how.html:
• Extraction: compress many features into a few (PCA) to fight the curse of dimensionality.
  • Selection: drop redundant or irrelevant columns (name, date of birth when age exists).
  • Construction: build new ones, e.g. customer lifetime = last purchase − first purchase.

how.title: Transform: bins and codes
how.html:
Binning turns numbers into groups (age 0–10, 11–20, or youth/adult/senior). Equal-width bins are simple; equal-frequency bins handle skewed data better.

Encoding turns categories into numbers: one-hot makes a 0/1 column per category; label encoding assigns 1, 2, 3, which wrongly implies an order for nominal data. Messy data like "Gas" vs "gas" creates fake categories, so clean before you encode.

demo.html:
Pre-filled with the self-study exercise. Edit the numbers, switch between the IQR fence and the 3-sigma rule, and change the multiplier. Red points fall outside the fence.

Try adding a huge value like 500 and watch how it drags the mean and standard deviation (and so the 3-sigma fence) but barely moves the IQR fence. That's why IQR is the more robust choice for small or skewed data.

example.html:
Bank customer segmentation. A bank wants to segment customers for targeted marketing and later target high-income customers with premium cards. Its table mixes attribute types: gender (nominal), service rating (ordinal), card type (ordinal), credit score (continuous), "is priority customer" (binary), region (nominal).

Student records. A programme office wants to predict next-semester GPA to estimate how many students will reach their dissertation. That means selecting relevant columns (drop name, birth date, batch), constructing semester totals, and encoding completion flags.

misunderstandings: Sometimes they are the signal (fraud, intrusion). Investigate before removing.

takeaways: Know each attribute's type (nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio; discrete or continuous) before choosing methods.
Data quality issues are noise, outliers, wrong/fake values, missing values and duplicates.
Clean, aggregate, and impute deliberately; detect outliers with IQR or 3-sigma.
Use representative, stratified samples; fix imbalance by under- or over-sampling.
Scale features (fit on training data only) and engineer them: extract, select, construct, bin, encode.
thirty: Preprocessing turns raw data into model-ready features. First identify attribute types and data types. Then fix quality problems: clean errors and inconsistencies, fill missing values sensibly, remove duplicates, and detect outliers with the IQR fence or the 3-sigma rule. Split data into representative training, validation and test sets, stratifying and rebalancing where needed. Finally scale numeric features, fitting the scaler on training data only, and engineer features by extracting, selecting, constructing, binning and encoding them.

check.q: Temperature in °C is which attribute type?
check.why: Differences are meaningful but 0 °C is not a true zero.

check.q: Where should you fit a scaler?
check.why: Fit on training data, then transform both training and test data.

check.q: Q1 = 10 and Q3 = 20. Which value is an outlier by the 1.5 × IQR rule?
check.why: Fences are −5 and 35, so 36 is outside.

check.q: Fraud is 0.5% of transactions. A common fix in the training set is…
opts: Over-sample fraud or under-sample normal cases
check.why: Rebalance so the rare class is well represented.
